items.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewee discusses Dizzy Gillespie's role in bebop and compares him to Charlie Parker and Miles Davis, but does not mention any direct personal interaction, collaboration, or professional relationship with Dizzy.

ctx.x: So what about Dizzy’s contribution to bebop?

Overwhelming in many ways, and actually Dizzy was responsible for making bebop a popular form because Bird was not that interested in fomenting a real interest in this kind of new music, he was just playing it. He never expected it to be that potent or important, but Diz did, Diz saw that thing that he could develop into a, in fact, I think it was Dizzy that called it bebop, I don’t think it was Bird.

items.title: Buddy DeFranco interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: Buddy was a member of Count Basie’s small band in the early ‘50s and soon after embraced the new style of jazz pioneered by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie.

ctx.x: What did the record companies, what did they think of bebop?

Most of them didn’t like it. They didn’t understand it or they didn’t like it. It’s only when bebop caught on with Dizzy and Bird and Jazz at the Philharmonic that record companies © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

began to say well maybe there’s something there. Norman Granz had his own record companies and began selling records like mad. And so they got in on that. But most of the company executives, in almost any area, didn’t know what they were recording. I hate to say that, but it’s pretty close to the truth. Very few. Very few really knew, good or bad.
